INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

🚨I have the same issues as last time when the DMK created the @tn_factcheck unit.

👉A party’s IT wing cannot become the State’s “Ministry of Truth.”

Renaming the Tamil Nadu Fact Check Unit as the “Information Integrity Desk” does not cure the fundamental conflict of interest. 

A government-controlled body cannot credibly claim independence when reported party social-media and IT-wing functionaries are placed in charge of deciding what is “true,” “false” or “misleading.” 

Mr "Guru Thalaiva" is reportedly TVK’s fan-club founder and he is the chief, with TVK IT-wing coordinator Dhivya appointed as a special officer. 

🔺The constitutional warning is already before us. On 21 March 2024, the Supreme Court stayed the Union government’s notification establishing its Fact Check Unit, observing that the challenge raised “serious constitutional questions” and that its impact on the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression required examination. 

The Bombay High Court subsequently struck down the underlying rule as unconstitutional, finding it vague, arbitrary and capable of chilling speech. In March 2026, the Supreme Court issued notice on the Union government’s appeal but refused to stay the High Court judgment. 

💡So, @TVKVijayHQ must answer:

What Government Order created this desk? What are the prescribed qualifications? Was there an open selection process? What expertise do the appointees possess in journalism, law, digital forensics, data verification or public administration? Have they relinquished their party positions? What safeguards prevent criticism of TVK from being branded “misinformation”?

A party publicity operation cannot simply be renamed an “Information Integrity Desk” and funded by taxpayers. 

Until the TVK Govt publishes the selection records, credentials, conflict-of-interest rules and limits of its powers, citizens are justified in viewing this not as independent fact-checking, but as political narrative management wearing an official badge.

Strategic Predictive Analysis :::
Pi Network: Could It Become Humanity’s Distributed Economic Operating System for Trading “Verified Data”?
(( When Data Itself Is No Longer the Asset, but “Verified Reality” Becomes the Asset — The Possibility of Integrating Humans, Businesses, AI, Machines, and Real-World Assets Into a Single Trusted Data Market ))

* [[[ This article includes Predictive & Technical Analysis  and may differ from actual outcomes ]]]

[[[ If the Internet connected information, the next economy may connect verified reality — Identity → Ownership → Data → Verification → Transaction → Settlement. ]]]

[[[ Pi’s true product may not be the coin itself, but the trustworthy state data generated by verified humans, businesses, AI, and machines. ]]]

[[[ The strongest AI may not be the one with the most data, but the one with continuous access to the largest body of verifiable real-world data. ]]]

[[[ From trading money to trading verified states of reality — energy, labor, ownership, production, contribution, and AI output could all become economically tradable verified data. ]]]

-----
1. Introduction — Is the Essence of Pi Network Really the “Coin”?

If Pi Network is viewed merely as a cryptocurrency project, many of its components can appear disconnected.

Why is KYC so important?

Why is KYB necessary?

Why does the application ecosystem matter?

Why are nodes necessary?

Why is AI relevant?

Why could RWA become important?

Why are ownership and contribution repeatedly emphasized?

Why might verified participation matter more than the transaction itself?

But if all of these elements are viewed through a single lens, the architecture becomes much simpler.

The essence of Pi Network may be a distributed economic platform for trading verified data.

The key word is not data.

It is verified data.

The Internet already contains an overwhelming amount of data.

The problem is that much of it cannot easily answer several fundamental questions.

Who created it?

Was it created by a real human?

Was it generated by AI?

Has it been manipulated?

Who owns it?

Who has permission to use it?

Which real-world asset does it correspond to?

When was it created?

Has it been modified since?

In other words, the fundamental problem of today’s Internet is increasingly not a shortage of information.

It is the trustworthiness of information.

The next economy may therefore evolve around converting trustworthiness itself into economic value.

-----
2. If the Internet Reduced the Cost of Transmitting Information, the Next Stage May Reduce the Cost of Verification

The great achievement of the Internet was making information almost costless to copy and distribute.

But the Internet did not solve one critical problem:

Is this information actually true?

News can be copied.

Images can be copied.

Documents can be copied.

AI-generated content can be created at nearly unlimited scale.

Yet as the cost of reproducing information approaches zero, the cost of determining what is genuine may rise.

The scarce resource is therefore no longer information itself.

It is:

trustworthy information.

When blockchain, KYC, KYB, digital signatures, smart contracts, zero-knowledge proofs, distributed ledgers, and AI verification are combined, they could create an entirely new data layer.

If the Internet was primarily an:

Information Network

the next stage could become a:

Verified Reality Network

If Pi Network eventually evolves in this direction, its most important function may not be issuing currency.

It may be digitally verifying reality itself.

-----
3. Nearly Everything in an Economy Is Ultimately “State Data”

At a sufficiently abstract level, most economic activity is data.

A bank balance is data describing:

who owns how much.

A land registry describes:

who owns which property.

A share of stock describes:

who owns what percentage of economic rights in a company.

An electricity meter records:

who produced or consumed how much electricity.

Logistics records:

which object moved from where to where, and when.

Labor records:

who performed what work and how much.

Taxation also depends on data describing:

which economic event occurred and which public costs must be settled.

At a deep level, economic activity can therefore be described as:

State Change

Ownership changed.

Energy was produced.

A service was provided.

A product was delivered.

An AI completed a task.

A robot completed an operation.

Each of these represents a change in the state of the real world.

If that state change can be reliably verified, it can itself become an economic asset.

-----
4. In a Pi-Type Economy, What Is Actually Being Traded May Be “Verified State”

In a traditional cryptocurrency system, the central event is usually the movement of tokens.

A sends 10 tokens to B.

In a fully developed verification economy, transactions become much richer.

For example:

A person was verified as a real human.

A company was verified as a legitimate producer.

A power plant actually generated 10 MWh of electricity.

An AI agent genuinely completed a specified task.

A product was actually delivered.

Ownership of a property was legally transferred.

A medical service was genuinely provided.

A node reliably maintained the network for a specified period.

Every one of these is a verified state transition.

The role of Pi then changes.

Pi does not necessarily have to be the object being traded.

It can become:

the economic settlement unit for verified changes in reality.

In that sense, Pi would not merely be money used to buy data.

It could function as a protocol-level unit for converting verified changes in the real world into economic rights.

-----
5. KYC May Be Much More Than a Regulatory Procedure

In conventional finance, KYC is often perceived merely as a compliance burden.

In a verification economy, however, KYC takes on an entirely different meaning.

KYC becomes:

the first anchor proving that the origin of a data contribution is a real human being.

Consider an online product review.

A statement such as:

“This person used this product”

can easily be fabricated.

But if the system can verify that a real person:

actually purchased the product,
actually used it,
and actually submitted the review,

the value of that data changes dramatically.

KYC therefore has the potential to become more than an AML mechanism.

It could become a:

Human-Origin Data Verification Layer

If that layer eventually extends across hundreds of millions or even billions of people, its economic significance could be enormous.

-----
6. KYB Connects Business Data to the Real World
If KYC verifies humans, KYB verifies businesses and organizations.

Does the company actually exist?

What does it produce?

Who is accountable for it?

Under which legal jurisdiction does it operate?

What assets does it own?

Once these facts are verified, the data produced by the business can also be anchored to reality.

Therefore:

Verified Human
Verified Business

creates a much more reliable economic data environment than anonymous Internet data.

If sensors, IoT devices, robots, and AI systems are then incorporated, a third layer emerges:

Verified Machine

-----
7. The Network Could Ultimately Become an Economy of Verified Humans, Businesses, Machines, and AI

A mature architecture could contain four principal economic actors:

humans,
businesses,
machines,
AI.

All of them produce data.

Humans generate data about:
consumption,
labor,
evaluation,
creativity,
contribution.
Businesses generate data about:

production,
revenue,
inventory,
logistics,
services.

Machines generate data about:

energy production,
transportation,
manufacturing,
environmental measurement,
sensor activity.

AI generates data about:

analysis,
prediction,
design,
code,
decisions.

If all of these data streams become verifiable, the economy itself begins to resemble one enormous real-time state market.

-----
8. This Changes the Value of AI Completely
Today, AI competition is usually framed around:
GPUs,
model size,
parameter count,
training data.
But over the longer term, a more important competition may emerge:

Who has access to the largest amount of verified reality?

Internet data contains misinformation, manipulation, duplication, stale information, and synthetic content.

There is also a growing problem of AI systems training on content generated by other AI systems.
By contrast:
Verified Human Data
Verified Business Data
Verified Machine Data
Verified Transaction Data
Verified Ownership Data
could become exceptionally high-quality material for AI.
The future competition for superintelligence may therefore not depend only on the number of GPUs available.

It may depend on:

access to trustworthy real-world data.

-----
9. This May Be the Deeper Reason Why Pi and AI Could Converge
It would be too narrow to describe the relationship between Pi and AI simply as:
“a blockchain using AI features.”
A deeper relationship could be:

Pi verifies reality, while AI interprets reality.

A Pi-type network records:
what actually happened.
AI analyzes:
what those events mean.
The combination becomes:

**Verification Layer
Intelligence Layer**

That is fundamentally different from an ordinary AI chatbot.

-----
10. RWA Is Ultimately the Financialization of Verified Reality Data
RWA becomes much easier to understand through this framework.
What is an oil RWA?
Verified data representing the existence of a certain quantity of oil or a legal claim on future oil production.

What is a real-estate RWA?

Verified data representing ownership or income rights associated with a specific property.

What is an energy RWA?

Verified data representing the right to consume, receive, or sell a specified amount of future energy.

What is a tokenized Treasury security?
Verified data representing a legal claim on a government obligation.
In other words, an RWA is not the physical object itself.
It is:

verifiable rights data anchored to a real-world asset.

Once such rights are connected to blockchain infrastructure, almost any real-world asset can potentially become digitally transferable.

-----
11. The Meaning of Ownership Could Expand Dramatically

In the traditional economy, ownership has largely centered on assets such as:

homes,
land,
shares,
cash.

In a data economy, ownership could extend to:
data rights,
AI-training contribution rights,
energy production rights,
network contribution rights,
intellectual property,
compute contribution rights.
That means nearly every form of value created by a human being could potentially be associated with an economic right.
This would represent an important shift from a labor-centered economy toward an ownership-centered economy.

-----
12. Labor Itself Could Become Verified Data

In the traditional labor economy:

a company evaluates labor
and pays wages.

In a distributed verification economy, it may become possible to directly measure:

actual contribution,
output,
quality,
usage,
utility.

Compensation could then become linked not merely to hours worked but to:

Verified Contribution

This could change the employment relationship itself.

A person would no longer necessarily need to belong to a specific company in order to participate economically.

Instead, the individual could:

contribute directly to a network,
have that contribution verified,
and receive economic rights in return.

-----
13. Data Trading Could Become Value Trading

It is important to clarify that “trading data” does not have to mean selling personal information.

An ideal architecture would do the opposite.

Private information could remain protected while the user proves only the necessary fact.

For example:

prove that someone is an adult without revealing the exact birth date.
prove that a person satisfies an income requirement without disclosing exact income.
prove ownership of a qualifying asset without revealing the entire portfolio.

prove possession of a qualification without exposing the full identity record.

This is the core logic of zero-knowledge verification.

The economy would therefore shift from:

Data Disclosure

toward:

Proof of Data

That distinction is fundamental.

-----
14. A Data Economy Could Exist Without Selling Personal Privacy

Much of today’s Internet economy works roughly like this:

collect user behavior data
→ store it centrally
→ use it for advertising and recommendations
→ platform monetizes it.

A future verification economy could reverse that structure.

Individual owns the data
→ proves only what is necessary
→ directly grants access permission
→ receives part of the resulting value

This would represent a transition from:

Platform-Owned Data Economy

to:

User-Owned Verified Data Economy

That could become one of the defining characteristics of a supra-sovereign ownership-based economy.

-----
15. This Could Also Explain Why Pi Might Become Economically Scarce

The value of Pi cannot be explained adequately through token supply alone.

But if Pi becomes involved in settling verified state changes among:
humans,
businesses,
machines,
AI,
real-world assets,
the scale of economic value exchanged across the network could become far larger than the nominal quantity of Pi itself.
In other words:

Verified Economic Activity

could grow much faster than:
Pi Supply
In such a scenario, Pi could evolve beyond a transactional coin and function more like:
a global settlement claim on verified utility.

-----
16. Differential Internal Purchasing Power Can Also Be Reinterpreted Through the Data-Economy Lens
The hypothesis we previously examined — that different contributors might experience different internal purchasing power — becomes more understandable in this framework.

The same nominal 1 Pi could potentially be associated with different economic histories.

For example:

How was it acquired?
How long did the person participate?
What data or contribution was provided?
What ownership rights are attached?
What provenance can be verified?

Economic value may therefore become more complex than the account balance alone.

Instead of:

Balance
the true state could become:

Balance + Provenance + Contribution + Rights

If implemented, that would represent a far richer expression of economic value than a traditional bank balance.

-----
17. Taxation Could Also Become Real-Time Data Settlement
If economic activity becomes a sequence of verified state transitions, taxation could also change.
Today, taxation commonly works through:
income reporting,
accounting,
tax calculation,
retrospective verification.

If transactions and resource use are verified in real time, public costs could potentially be settled when:

production occurs,
consumption occurs,
resources are used,
externalities are created.

This would shift taxation from:

After-the-Fact Taxation

toward:

Real-Time Economic Settlement
The administrative cost of taxation itself could fall substantially.

-----
18. The State Could Move From Being an Information Monopoly Toward Being a Verified Public-Service Provider

Traditional states control large amounts of critical information:

identity,
property records,
business registration,
taxes,
licenses,
ownership records,
qualifications.

In a supra-sovereign verification network, some of these functions could become protocolized.

The state would not disappear.

Its role could change.

It could focus increasingly on:

legal finality,
public safety,
dispute resolution,
public infrastructure,
externality management.

The transition would be from:

State as Information Monopoly

toward:

State as Verified Public Service Provider

-----
19. Businesses Could Also Shift From Data Monopoly Toward Service Competition

Much of the power of today’s platform companies comes from data.

They know:

what people purchase,
where they travel,
what they search,
who they communicate with.

That information is usually stored on centralized corporate servers.

If individuals directly control their verified data, platform monopoly power could weaken.

Companies would move from being:

powerful because they own the data

toward being:
chosen because they provide the best service.
Competition would therefore become more directly connected to utility.

-----
20. AI Companies Would Not Be Exempt From This Transformation

Large-scale data is one of the primary competitive assets of current AI companies.

But if verified data remains owned by individuals and networks, AI companies may no longer be able to extract it unilaterally.
Instead, they may need to:
purchase data-access rights,
provide useful outputs,
share resulting value.
AI itself would move from:

Data Extractor

toward:

Data Market Participant

This could fundamentally change the ownership structure of the AI economy.

-----
21. This Architecture Becomes Even More Important in a Robot Economy

Robots continuously generate real-world data.

They generate information about:

location,
battery condition,
completed work,
sensors,
production volume,
service time.

If these records are trustworthy, robots can participate economically with far less direct human supervision.

For example:
Work Completed
→ Data Submitted
→ Verification
→ Automatic Settlement
Machines themselves begin to function as economic actors.
A Pi-type verification network could therefore connect humans and machines within the same economic protocol.

-----
22. Money Could Gradually Become a “Claim on Verified Data”

Traditional money is largely sustained through institutional and sovereign trust.

A future protocol currency could derive more of its value from measurable economic reality.

For example:

How many real humans participate?
How many real assets are connected?
How much production occurs?
How many verified transactions exist?
How many AI systems and machines provide actual services?

Money could gradually evolve from:

Store of Abstract Trust

toward:

Claim on Verified Economic Reality

That could become part of Pi’s long-term significance.

-----
23. Verified Data May Become the New Fundamental Resource

The Industrial Revolution depended heavily on:

coal,
iron,
oil.

The information age elevated:
data.
The AI era may go one step further.
Its defining resource may become:
Verified Data

Ordinary data can be created almost without limit.

Verified reality cannot.

A real human contribution,

real electricity produced by a power plant,

a real product manufactured by a company,

a real task completed by a robot,

a real experience recorded by a human,

cannot simply be duplicated without limit.

They are scarce.

The truly strategic resource of the future may therefore be:

Verifiable Reality

-----
24. This Could Create Humanity’s First Global Market for Verified Reality
If billions of people, businesses, machines, and AI systems eventually operate within one interoperable verification framework, a very unusual market could emerge.
In such a market:

money,
labor,
energy,
data,
AI,
ownership,
assets,
services

would no longer necessarily exist as entirely separate economic domains.
They would all become:
transactions in verified changes of state.
The result could resemble a:

Global Market for Verified Reality

-----
25. Pi Network’s True Competitors May Not Be Other Cryptocurrencies

If this interpretation is correct, comparing Pi only with Bitcoin, Ethereum, or Solana would be far too narrow.

The actual competitive domains could include:

Google’s data layer,
Amazon’s commerce infrastructure,
Visa’s payments network,
SWIFT’s financial messaging,
banks’ identity and credit systems,
governments’ registries and identity infrastructure,
cloud computing networks,
AI companies’ data ecosystems.

All of these systems share a common feature:

trusted state information is managed by a centralized institution.

A distributed verification network would attempt to move some of that function into protocol infrastructure.

-----
26. Pi’s Ultimate Value Could Depend More on “Verification Density” Than Transaction Volume
Blockchains usually compete using metrics such as TPS.
But raw TPS may not be enough in the future.
A more important question could be:
How much of the activity is connected to real, verified economic reality?
One hundred million bot transactions may be economically less valuable than one million genuine human economic transactions.
A more meaningful future metric could therefore be:

Verified Economic States Per Second

rather than merely:

Transactions Per Second

We could call this:

Verification Density
The higher the verification density, the greater the economic trustworthiness of the network.

-----
27. Ultimately, the Network Could Become a Distributed Economic Database for Humanity
In its most advanced form, a Pi-type system would not merely be a payment network or blockchain.
It could become a distributed economic data layer capable of proving — while protecting privacy as much as possible:

who a person is,
what they own,
what they produced,
what they consumed,
what they contributed,
what rights they possess.

No central government,

bank,

corporation,

or AI company

would necessarily own the entire system.

It could instead evolve toward a:

Humanity-Owned Economic Data Layer

-----
28. If Superintelligent AI Operates on Top of This Layer, the Economy Itself Could Begin to Learn
Once verified data continuously enters the system and AI analyzes it, the economy itself can become adaptive.
The loop could look like this:
Production → Data
Consumption → Data
Contribution → Data
Resource Conditions → Data
AI Analysis → Optimization
Policy and Production Adjustment
→ New Data

This creates a self-amplifying cycle:

Economic Activity → Verified Data → AI Learning → Better Economic Coordination → More Economic Activity

At that point, the economy begins to resemble something far beyond a system manually maintained by human institutions.

It approaches a:

Self-Learning Economic Operating System

-----
29. Strategic Forecast — The Final Competition May Not Be About Who Has the Most Money

The competitive power of nations and corporations could also change.

Today, the dominant metrics include:

GDP,
capital,
industrial capacity,
energy.

In the future, another metric may become critical:

How much verifiable real-world data can a system economically connect and coordinate?

In the AI era:

verified data improves AI quality,
AI improves economic efficiency,
greater efficiency increases utility,

greater utility attracts more participation,

and more participation creates more verified data.

The loop becomes:

Verified Data ↑
→ AI Intelligence ↑
→ Economic Efficiency ↑
→ Utility ↑
→ Participation ↑
→ More Verified Data ↑

That could become an extraordinarily powerful network effect.

------------------------
30. Conclusion — Pi’s Real Asset May Not Be Pi, but “Verifiable Reality”
------------------------
If Pi Network is viewed only as a cryptocurrency, the central question becomes:

What will the price of Pi be?

But if it is viewed as a distributed market for verified human and economic data, the questions change completely.

How many humans are verified?
How many businesses are connected?
How many real-world assets are verifiable?
How many AI systems and machines perform real economic activity?
How many changes in real-world state can be recorded with trustworthy provenance?
Those become the critical metrics.

In that framework, the ultimate role of Pi can be described as follows:

Pi may not merely be digital money.
It may become a protocol asset connecting economic rights in a world where verified states of reality can be owned, exchanged, and settled.

In even simpler terms:
The real commodity is not Pi.
The real commodity is verified reality.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. New Delhi is asking a question Starlink can't really answer: given its US ownership and global network, how can it promise to follow Indian rules when Washington wants the opposite?

What spooked them is concrete. Starlink terminals were used in the Iran war even though it holds no license in Iran. India watched a sovereign state fail to switch off a network running over its own territory, and asked who is next.

Notice the tell. Jio and Bharti get an easier ride because their satellite partners are European, not a US-controlled operator. The worry isn't the satellites, it's whose hand is on the switch. And it lands days before SpaceX's IPO at a $1.75tn valuation, with Starlink as the main revenue engine, a reminder that the global rollout is far from uniform: shut out of China, and now stuck in India too.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

NEEM KAROLI BABA
📷

The Life, Teachings and Enduring Legacy of Maharaj-ji
Neem Karoli Baba—also written as Neeb Karori Baba and affectionately called Maharaj-ji by his followers—was one of the most influential Indian spiritual teachers of the twentieth century. A deeply devoted follower of Lord Hanuman, he became known for a remarkably simple spiritual message centred on love, devotion to God, compassion, feeding people and selfless service.
Although he died in 1973, his influence has continued to expand. His ashrams attract large numbers of devotees, while his teachings have travelled far beyond India through disciples such as Ram Dass. His name has also become associated with prominent international figures including Steve Jobs and Mark Zuckerberg, while Indian public figures such as Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma have visited sites associated with him. The extraordinary success of the 2026 film Hanuman Ansh, inspired by his life, has introduced Maharaj-ji to another generation. It is more accurate to say that Neem Karoli Baba is revered by a very large community of devotees in India and abroad, rather than that he is worshipped by all Indians. For devotees, however, Maharaj-ji is much more than a historical religious teacher: many regard him as a saint, siddha or divinely realised being.

EARLY LIFE
The precise details of Neem Karoli Baba's early years are not completely certain, and different devotional biographies sometimes give different versions. He is generally believed to have been born around 1900 in Uttar Pradesh. His birth name is usually given as Lakshman Narayan Sharma (with variations in spelling in different accounts). He was born into a Brahmin family and was married at a young age, as was customary in many parts of India at that time. Accounts of his life describe an early attraction towards spirituality and renunciation. He left home for periods of wandering and spiritual practice. Eventually, at his father's request, he returned to family life. He became the father of two sons and a daughter, demonstrating an unusual combination of the roles of householder and wandering holy man. Over the years he travelled widely across northern India and became known by several names.

HOW HE BECAME "NEEM KAROLI BABA"
One of the most famous stories concerning Maharaj-ji explains the origin of the name by which the world eventually knew him. According to the traditional account, he was once travelling on a train without a ticket and was ordered to get off near the village of Neeb Karori/Neem Karoli in Uttar Pradesh. After he left the train, the locomotive supposedly would not move despite repeated attempts. The story says that railway officials eventually requested the sadhu to return to the train. He agreed, reportedly on conditions that included treating holy men respectfully and establishing a railway stop for local people. According to devotees' accounts, once he reboarded, the train started moving again. This incident became one of the most frequently repeated stories associated with him and helped establish the name Neem Karoli Baba. It is important, however, to distinguish devotional tradition from independently verifiable history. The train episode and many similar stories are central to the oral tradition surrounding Maharaj-ji, but should not automatically be treated as scientifically or historically established miracles. The new film Hanuman Ansh also incorporates the famous train story into its depiction of his life.

DEVOTION TO LORD HANUMAN
At the centre of Neem Karoli Baba's spiritual life was an intense devotion to Lord Hanuman, the great devotee of Lord Rama in the Ramayana. Hanuman represents strength, humility, courage, absolute devotion and selfless service. These qualities are also central to the way Maharaj-ji's followers understand his teachings. He encouraged devotion to God, remembrance of the divine name and service to human beings. Temples dedicated to Hanuman became closely associated with the ashrams established around him. Rather than developing a complicated new religious philosophy, Maharaj-ji emphasised direct spiritual practice and compassionate living. His teachings are frequently summarised through the ideas: Love everyone. Serve everyone. Feed people. Remember God.This simplicity became one of the reasons his teachings could appeal to people from very different cultural and religious backgrounds.

MAHARAJ-JI'S STYLE OF TEACHING
Neem Karoli Baba was very different from a conventional religious lecturer. He did not become famous for lengthy philosophical discourses or for establishing an elaborate theological system. Much of what is known about his teachings comes instead from the recollections of people who spent time with him. His approach emphasised bhakti—devotion and love of God. For him, spirituality was closely connected with practical compassion. Feeding a hungry person, serving someone in difficulty, remembering God and treating other people with love could themselves become forms of spiritual practice. His followers also remember him as someone who discouraged excessive attachment to his own personality. Despite the enormous devotional following that eventually grew around him, the image preserved by disciples is of a guru who preferred simplicity and avoided elaborate self-promotion.

KAINCHI DHAM
The place most strongly associated with Neem Karoli Baba today is Kainchi Dham, situated in the Kumaon hills of Uttarakhand near Nainital. The ashram was established in 1964 and became one of the principal centres connected with Maharaj-ji. Surrounded by mountains and forest, Kainchi Dham developed into an important spiritual destination. The complex contains temples associated with Hanuman and Maharaj-ji and continues to receive devotees from India and overseas. Its annual celebrations attract large crowds, and the remarkable international reputation of the ashram is partly connected to the Western disciples and visitors influenced by Maharaj-ji. The success of Hanuman Ansh in 2026 has created renewed public interest in Maharaj-ji and places associated with his life. Recent reporting has described another surge of visitors seeking locations connected with him.

RAM DASS AND THE SPREAD OF MAHARAJ-JI'S TEACHINGS IN THE WEST
Perhaps no individual did more to introduce Neem Karoli Baba to Western audiences than Ram Dass, originally known as Dr Richard Alpert. Alpert had been a Harvard psychologist and was closely associated with Timothy Leary and the psychedelic experimentation of the 1960s. He travelled to India in 1967, where he encountered Neem Karoli Baba. Maharaj-ji gave him the name Ram Dass, meaning "servant of God." The encounter fundamentally changed the direction of his life. Ram Dass subsequently became an influential spiritual teacher in the United States. His landmark 1971 book Be Here Now introduced large numbers of Western readers to Indian spirituality and helped spread awareness of Neem Karoli Baba. Through Ram Dass and other disciples, a spiritual teacher who himself never became an international travelling guru acquired an extraordinary international following.

MIRACLES AND STORIES ASSOCIATED WITH MAHARAJ-JI
An important part of Neem Karoli Baba's reputation concerns the many extraordinary experiences reported by his devotees. Followers have attributed to him abilities such as apparently knowing people's thoughts or circumstances without being told, appearing to possess knowledge of distant events, healing or helping people during crises, producing unexpectedly large quantities of food, and influencing circumstances in ways devotees regarded as miraculous. The railway story is perhaps the most famous example. For believers, these accounts demonstrate Maharaj-ji's spiritual attainment. From a historical or scientific perspective, however, many such stories cannot be independently verified and largely come from disciples, eyewitness recollections and devotional literature.
This distinction is important. One can understand the importance of the miracle tradition to Neem Karoli Baba's followers without presenting every supernatural claim as an independently established fact. Maharaj-ji's deeper legacy arguably rests less on miracle stories than on the values repeatedly associated with him: love, seva, compassion, devotion and feeding those in need.

HIS INTERNATIONAL AND CELEBRITY FOLLOWING
One of the most fascinating as pects of Neem Karoli Baba's legacy is the influence associated with him among prominent Western spiritual seekers, entrepreneurs, artists and philanthropists.
Ram Dass -Ram Dass actually met Neem Karoli Baba and became his disciple. His writings and lectures were crucial in carrying Maharaj-ji's teachings to the Western world.
Steve Jobs- The connection with Apple co-founder Steve Jobs needs an important clarification. Jobs travelled to India in 1974, seeking spiritual understanding and hoping to encounter Neem Karoli Baba. However, Maharaj-ji had already died in September 1973. Jobs therefore did not personally meet Neem Karoli Baba. Jobs nevertheless travelled to the Kainchi region and spent time exploring Indian spirituality. His travelling companion Daniel Kottke later recalled arriving at the Neem Karoli ashram after Maharaj-ji's death and finding it largely deserted. Thus, statements sometimes circulated online that Jobs personally received Neem Karoli Baba's blessings should be treated cautiously. The documented connection is that Jobs travelled to India seeking him and encountered the spiritual environment associated with him after his death.
Mark Zuckerberg -The connection later extended to Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg. Zuckerberg has spoken publicly about travelling in India during a difficult period in Facebook's early history. According to accounts of the episode, Steve Jobs encouraged him to visit the temple associated with the spiritual tradition that Jobs himself had encountered in India. Zuckerberg subsequently visited Kainchi Dham. This created an extraordinary symbolic link between a relatively secluded Himalayan spiritual centre and two generations of Silicon Valley entrepreneurs.
Julia Roberts -Hollywood actress Julia Roberts has also been associated with Neem Karoli Baba's influence. Reports about her spiritual journey have linked her interest in Hinduism to encountering an image of Maharaj-ji. Some popular accounts go further and claim repeated visits to Kainchi Dham, although the details are less firmly documented than the Ram Dass connection and should therefore be stated with appropriate caution.
Larry Brilliant -Another significant follower was American physician and public-health figure Dr Larry Brilliant. Brilliant spent time with Maharaj-ji and later became deeply involved in international efforts against smallpox. Accounts from Brilliant's life describe Maharaj-ji encouraging him to become involved with the international smallpox-eradication effort. His story is especially interesting because it connects Maharaj-ji's idea of seva—service—to practical humanitarian work.
Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma -In recent years, Indian cricketer Virat Kohli and actor Anushka Sharma have also been prominently associated in media reports with visits to places connected with Neem Karoli Baba. Their visits contributed to renewed interest in Maharaj-ji among younger Indians, although visiting an ashram should not automatically be interpreted as formal discipleship. Other prominent Western visitors and admirers have also been linked with the wider Neem Karoli Baba spiritual tradition. Reporting on Kainchi Dham has noted its unusual attraction for members of the American technology community.

DEATH OF NEEM KAROLI BABA
Neem Karoli Baba died on 11 September 1973 in Vrindavan. Accounts state that he had experienced health problems and was taken to a hospital in Vrindavan, where he died during the early hours of 11 September. For devotees, his physical death did not represent the end of his spiritual presence. His temples, ashrams and communities continued functioning, while the books and memories of disciples introduced him to people who had never met him during his lifetime. In that sense, his international reputation actually expanded considerably after his death.

HANUMAN ANSH: THE 2026 FILM INSPIRED BY NEEM KAROLI BABA
The extraordinary revival of interest in Maharaj-ji in 2026 is closely connected with the Hindi devotional film Hanuman Ansh. Directed and written by Vishal Chaturvedi, the film was released in cinemas on 7 August 2026. It dramatises the spiritual journey of Neem Karoli Baba, beginning with his earlier life and moving towards his emergence as the spiritual figure remembered as Maharaj-ji. The film features Shobinaw Satyaa in the central role associated with Neem Karoli Baba, with Chandan Anand and an ensemble cast including Nikhil Dubey, Udaysinh Rajput, Purnima Tiwari and Mannish Chaudhary. The production itself had an unusual history. Director Vishal Chaturvedi has said that the project represented many years of work and research. Shobinaw Satyaa was originally working on the production as an assistant director before circumstances led to him auditioning for the role of Maharaj-ji. According to his account, the transition from crew member to leading actor happened remarkably quickly. The filmmakers also faced considerable difficulties getting the project completed and distributed. Recent interviews describe financial problems, changes to the production team and rejection by an OTT platform before the film eventually reached cinemas.

An Unexpected Blockbuster
Hanuman Ansh began as a comparatively small production without the marketing machinery or star cast normally associated with a major Hindi blockbuster. Its performance then changed dramatically through word of mouth. By 19 September 2026, contemporary reporting described the film as having crossed approximately ₹300 crore worldwide, although different trade reports and publications have quoted somewhat different figures as its theatrical run has continued. That is particularly remarkable because contemporary reports place its production budget at only around ₹1.7–2 crore. The film therefore became one of 2026's most surprising Indian box-office stories. Its success is significant beyond cinema. It has introduced Neem Karoli Baba's life to audiences who may previously have known him only from social media photographs, stories about Steve Jobs, or references to Kainchi Dham. Some screenings have reportedly taken on an atmosphere resembling devotional gatherings, demonstrating how the boundary between religious experience and cinematic experience can become blurred when a film concerns a revered spiritual figure. The film should nevertheless be understood as a devotional cinematic interpretation inspired by Maharaj-ji's life, rather than as a documentary in which every scene should automatically be regarded as historically verified.

CONTROVERSIES AND QUESTIONS SURROUNDING NEEM KAROLI BABA
Compared with many modern religious personalities, Neem Karoli Baba himself is not associated in credible mainstream reporting with a major, well-established personal scandal.There are, however, several areas where controversy, disagreement or caution is appropriate.

1. Miracles versus Historical Evidence
Many of the most famous stories about Maharaj-ji—including the railway incident and accounts of supernatural knowledge—come from devotees and oral traditions. Followers regard them as evidence of divine grace or spiritual powers. A historical or secular examination must distinguish these accounts from events supported by independent contemporary documentation. This does not mean that the stories are meaningless. They are extremely important for understanding the faith surrounding Maharaj-ji. It simply means that faith claims and historically verifiable claims belong to different categories of evidence.

2. Exaggerated Celebrity Connections
Modern social media sometimes simplifies or exaggerates Maharaj-ji's relationships with famous people. Steve Jobs is the clearest example. Jobs went to India hoping to find Neem Karoli Baba, but Maharaj-ji had already died. Therefore, descriptions claiming that Jobs personally met Maharaj-ji or directly received his advice before creating Apple are inconsistent with the established chronology. Similarly, celebrity visits to an ashram do not necessarily establish that the visitor became a formal disciple.

3. Commercialisation and Social-Media "Miracle" Culture
Maharaj-ji's enormous contemporary popularity has produced a flood of online posts promising prosperity, marriage, employment, healing or other rewards in exchange for sharing his image or posting devotional phrases. This has itself attracted criticism. A 2026 Hindustan Times commentary argued that such internet claims risk turning genuine devotion into clickbait and presenting matters of faith as guaranteed formulas for material results. This phenomenon is especially noteworthy because the historical image of Maharaj-ji preserved by his followers is one of simplicity and lack of interest in personal publicity.

4. Dispute Concerning an Ancestral Property
A more concrete recent controversy concerns property associated with Neem Karoli Baba's family. In August 2026, six granddaughters from his family approached the Firozabad district administration regarding a dispute involving his ancestral home and a worship site. They made allegations concerning interference by the Shri Thakur Hanuman Ji Trust. The trust disputed the allegations, and authorities were examining records and competing claims. This is important to describe accurately: it is a property/trust dispute involving descendants and an organisation associated with the site, not evidence of wrongdoing by Neem Karoli Baba himself, who died more than five decades earlier.

5. The Difficulty of Separating Biography from Hagiography
A broader scholarly challenge is that much of what is popularly known about Maharaj-ji comes from disciples and devotional literature. Such accounts provide invaluable insight into how followers experienced him, but they naturally emphasise spiritual experiences and miracles. Consequently, any responsible biography should distinguish among, Documented biographical events; first-hand recollections of disciples; traditional stories; and explicitly supernatural claims accepted through faith. Doing so neither dismisses faith nor presents belief as historical proof.

WHY HIS MESSAGE CONTINUES TO ATTRACT PEOPLE
The enduring attraction of Neem Karoli Baba may ultimately be explained by the extraordinary simplicity of the spiritual ideal associated with him. His message did not require people to master complicated theology. It asked them to love, serve, remember God and care for other human beings. This allowed Maharaj-ji's teachings to cross cultural boundaries. A Hindu devotee could understand his life through bhakti and Hanuman. A Western spiritual seeker could encounter his teachings through Ram Dass. A humanitarian such as Larry Brilliant could interpret seva through public service. Modern visitors may simply experience Kainchi Dham as a place for contemplation and inner quiet. His influence therefore extends beyond any single category of religion, celebrity culture or popular spirituality.

NEEM KAROLI BABA AND MODERN INDIA
The extraordinary success of Hanuman Ansh demonstrates that Neem Karoli Baba is no longer merely a figure remembered by an older generation of devotees. More than fifty years after his death, he has acquired a substantial new audience. Social media, celebrity visits, international interest in Kainchi Dham and now cinema have transformed the scale of public attention surrounding him. The result is a fascinating combination of traditional Hindu bhakti and twenty-first-century global popular culture. At the same time, this popularity creates a responsibility to distinguish Maharaj-ji's documented teachings from commercial claims and internet mythology made in his name.

CONCLUSION
Neem Karoli Baba occupies an unusual place in modern Indian spiritual history. Born as Lakshman Narayan Sharma around the beginning of the twentieth century, he lived without building the kind of international organisation normally associated with globally famous gurus. He remained deeply connected with Hanuman bhakti, simplicity, service and personal encounters with devotees. Yet his influence travelled remarkably far. Ram Dass carried his memory into Western spiritual culture. Steve Jobs travelled to India seeking the guru, although he arrived after Maharaj-ji's death. Mark Zuckerberg later visited Kainchi Dham. Larry Brilliant connected his spiritual experience with a life of public service. Actors, athletes, entrepreneurs and ordinary pilgrims have continued to visit places associated with him.

Then, more than half a century after Maharaj-ji's death, Hanuman Ansh unexpectedly transformed his life into one of India's major cinematic stories of 2026. The small-budget devotional film grew through word of mouth into a blockbuster and created another wave of interest in his life and teachings. There are miraculous stories surrounding him that belong principally to the realm of devotion rather than independently verified history. There are also modern disputes over property associated with his legacy and legitimate concerns about social-media exaggeration and commercialisation. But these controversies have so far remained largely around his legacy rather than constituting a documented major personal scandal involving Maharaj-ji himself. Perhaps the most enduring explanation for his appeal is also the simplest. Behind the miracles, famous followers, pilgrimage centres and now a blockbuster film lies a message that requires very little explanation: 

Love people. Serve people. Feed people. Remember God.

For millions of devotees, that remains the essence of Neem Karoli Baba—Maharaj-ji—and the reason his influence continues to grow long after his physical life ended. I deliberately corrected a few widely repeated claims—especially the idea that Steve Jobs personally met Neem Karoli Baba. Jobs reached India in 1974, whereas Maharaj-ji died on 11 September 1973. That distinction will make the note more credible if you intend to publish it.

It has become fashionable these days to abuse IITs and their faculties. I get it, freedom of speech, healthy skepticism of institutions, all fair game. 

But before that fashionable takedown becomes the whole story, sit with this 1 fact for a second....

Right now, last month, IIT profs have put more free, peer-reviewed, university grade course content into the world than any other institution on the planet, and most Indians have never watched a single hour of it.

2001....

A handful of IIT directors come back from a trip to Carnegie Mellon, having seen an American prof build an entire functioning university around teaching people online. 

They are stunned enough to try replicating it for India, in engineering, at a scale nobody had attempted before.

The idea finally took shape under Atal Bihari Vajpayee's government. The man holding the HRD portfolio through that entire stretch, 1998-2004, was Murli Manohar Joshi, himself a physics prof before he was ever a minister. 

On January 26, 2003, months before NPTEL's own official rollout that year, Joshi Ji personally inaugurated a companion initiative, the Eklavya Technology Channel, explicitly built to beam actual IIT classrooms into homes across the country. 

7 IITs and the IISc quietly went live. 

No press conference most people remember. Just profs, cameras, and a govt that wrote the check for something nobody could fully prove would work.

The word "MOOC" did not even exist yet. Coursera and edX launched in 2012. 

The term was not even coined until 2008. NPTEL was already recording real lectures years before Silicon Valley invented free online university education and got magazine covers for it. 

India did not copy the MOOC revolution, it built one of the first drafts before anyone had a name for it.

Fast forward to now. 

NPTEL is the largest repository of engineering and science course content on Earth: 

- 56,000+ hours of lectures

-3,200+ courses

- a YouTube channel with 1.86B views and 5.6M subscribers

...built entirely by government-funded faculty, not a venture-backed edtech company. 

Not entertainment.... 

Thermodynamics. Signal processing. Soil mechanics. Quantum Mechanics. 

Built by profs people love to mock as "out of touch," "irrelevant," "stuck in an old system."

A student in rural Bihar with a smartphone has, right now, the same lecture an IIT KGP student sat through, free, no JEE rank required. 

And yet ask most students outside the IIT system if they have done a single NPTEL certification, and you will mostly get silence. 

Employers still do not weight it the way they weight a foreign MOOC certificate with a fraction of the rigor. The exact students this was built for often do not know it exists.

If a country builds the largest free reservoir of elite education on the planet, a decade ahead of everyone else, and barely drinks from it, is that the institution's failure / ours, for criticizing loudly and never once checking what is already free and sitting right there?

Criticize the IITs all you want, no institution should be above scrutiny. But this particular story deserves the same volume as the criticism. It just never gets it.

Statement against arbitrary content takedown and account restrictions faced by public representatives and journalists

Earlier today, @Meta restricted the Instagram accounts (“Platform”) of @AamAadmiParty (AAP), its national convener @ArvindKejriwal, and Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear), co-founder of @AltNews. 

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.

Press Release 

Women Journos Protest Attacks

Six angry young women faced the cameras at the Press Club in Delhi on Friday September 18, 2026. 

They were not activists, they were journalists determined to be heard by their peers and governments. 

The DUJ expresses its solidarity and complete support for the struggles of these courageous media women. 

Pooja Mathur set the tone at the meeting held by the Press Club of India, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Network of Women in Media to protest attacks on women journalists.

 Mathur spoke boldly of how she has been targetted by the UP government for her coverage of the bulldozing of a Saharanpur masjid on Sept. 6. Mathur said she was the first to report the demolition on her YouTube channel Red Chili Live. She interviewed the Imam of the mosque and took a video of the rubble. After that she received messages demanding that she delete the videos, followed by threats when she refused. An FIR has been filed against her. 

Mathur said courageously, "I was doing my job. I àm not afraid. I will not cry, I will make them cry." She also pointed out that women journalists like her are the voice and the inspiration of countless other women who dare not step out of home and raise their own voices against oppression.

Mathur also said to the big gathering present, "Do not dismiss us as just youtubers. We are serious journalists, we are qualified, we do our research before we go online."

Divya Srivastava spoke of how she was targetted after she dared to speak at a 'press conference' held by UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Sept 12. The CM spoke but took no questions. When Divya loudly called him out, asking him to hear her question, he simply walked away. This smàll incident was blown out of proportion with some fellow journalists warning her to go into hiding as she would now be under fire. She was trolled heavily, with threats, gaalis and allegations that she had been sent by a rival political party to ask questions.

"Why should I hide, journalism is not a crime," Mathur said. 

She said her job at a channel was now insecure as the channel owners were afraid of the backlash.

Bindu Romi Gujjar and Monika Singh, both independent journalists based in Delhi, were among the first to reach Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh after several Baiga tribal children died of disease in August 2026. They interviewed parents and relatives of the children. 

Gujjar described the trauma of witnessing funeral rites. She said there was only one primary health centre for 25 villages and the nearest hospital is 130 km away. No ambulance is available. She said that the deaths were caused by malaria, a treatable disease. She asked why no malaria vaccines are provided in malaria prone areas. 

Singh described conditions in the government hospital where 3 or 4 children were lying in each bed.

The journalists' documentation of 30 deaths, backed by Aadhar cards and other evidence, embarrassed the local administration which claimed there were only eight deaths. The reporters were shadowed for several days and threatened. The Superintendent of Police wanted them to meet him. They did not go. Two policemen came to their hotel room at 2 a.m. at night, she said. They began to fear for their lives. Eventually they left the hotel in the night and returned to Delhi.
 
Singh spoke of the conditions in the Baiga villages where there are no facilities, not even clean drinking water. She spoke of the hospital which the District Magistrate, she said, visited several days after the first deaths. She claimed that 34 children were discharged the day before his visit, more beds were supplied, bed linen changed and the entire hospital disinfected.
